subject: Accounting
title: Cost of Goods Sold
description: A short lesson to help you apply Cost of Goods Sold.

hook.text: A bakery sells a cake for $30. The flour, eggs, and butter cost $10. That $10 is COGS.

buildup.text: Cost of goods sold captures the direct costs of making the products a company sells.

discovery.text: Subtract COGS from revenue and you get gross profit—the first measure of profitability.

twist.text: A company with high revenue but higher COGS is losing money on every sale it makes.

climax.text: Managing COGS is critical—it determines whether the core business model works at all.

punchline.text: If making it costs more than selling it, you're done.

quiz.question: What does COGS measure?
options: Direct costs of producing goods sold

details.summary: Cost of goods sold on the income statement represents the direct costs of producing revenue—materials, labor, and manufacturing overhead. This topic explains how COGS is calculated, what it includes, and how it drives the critical gross profit metric investors watch.
details.whyItMatters: COGS is typically the largest single expense on an income statement. Understanding it reveals whether a company's core business operations are efficient and whether its pricing strategy is sustainable.
takeaways: COGS includes only costs directly tied to production—raw materials, production labor, and manufacturing overhead
Gross profit equals revenue minus COGS and measures the core profitability of products or services
Rising COGS as a percentage of revenue signals pricing pressure, supply chain issues, or production inefficiency

faq.question: What does cost of goods sold include?
faq.answer: COGS includes direct materials used in production, direct labor costs of workers producing goods, and manufacturing overhead directly tied to production like factory rent and equipment depreciation. It excludes selling expenses, administrative costs, and R&D.

faq.question: Why is tracking COGS important for investors?
faq.answer: COGS determines gross profit margin, which reveals how efficiently a company produces its products. A declining gross margin may indicate rising input costs, competitive pricing pressure, or production inefficiencies—all critical signals for evaluating business health.
